subtitle: "Paraguay"

## Overview

The Mbyá, also called Mbyá Guaraní, are a branch of the Guaraní people living across Paraguay, Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay. They are considered a subgroup of the Guaraní people alongside the Pai Tavytera, Eastern Bolivian Guaraní, Guarayos, and Chané. The Mbyá refer to themselves as *Nhandeva*, meaning “us” or “our people,” while their ritual name is *Jeguakava Tenonde Porangue'í*, meaning “the First Chosen to Carry the Sacred Adornment of Feathers” or “The First Adorned.” In Paraguay, census and other estimates recorded 5,500 Mbyá in 1981, 4,744 in 1992, 10,990 represented in 1995, and 12,100 in 2000. Their culture is marked by mobility, spoken transmission of knowledge, ritual life, forest-based subsistence, and distinctive material objects.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

They do state that the Mbyá’s ritual name refers to carrying or wearing a sacred adornment of feathers, but provide no further description of this adornment.

### Architecture

Mbyá villages are known as *tekoa*. Ideally, a *tekoa* is located where the traditional Mbyá way of life, called *ñande reko*, can be reproduced. Such villages are characterized by a traditional house of worship known as an *opy*, where rituals are performed. They are ideally surrounded by forests and fields and situated near a good water source, although this is not always possible for contemporary Mbyá communities.

They state that Mbyá individuals and families may move among villages and encampments, visiting relatives, spreading news, participating in rituals, and undertaking collective work such as constructing buildings.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Archaeological evidence connects the proto-Guaraní from whom the Mbyá descended with pottery and basket-weaving. They produced objects used to collect, prepare, and serve food. Archaeologists have found clay pots used as funeral urns, arrowheads, and other inorganic materials at proto-Guaraní archaeological sites.

The sources also mention the Mbyá’s production and sale of handicrafts. They state that products sold outside villages reference Mbyá material culture and cosmology.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The Mbyá ritual name *Jeguakava Tenonde Porangue'í* is translated as “the First Chosen to Carry the Sacred Adornment of Feathers” or “The First Adorned.”

## Music & performance

Music is connected with Mbyá ritual and collective gatherings. The sources state that the Mbyá and Nhandeva reproduced and used objects brought by the Jesuits, including musical instruments such as the *ravé*, identified as a *rabeca*, and the *mbaraká*, identified as a guitar.

Shamans lead ritual songs and dances. They also perform rituals intended to influence the weather, prevent future events, and ensure fruitful hunts and harvests. Ritual songs and dances are therefore connected with healing, spiritual authority, agriculture, hunting, and the work of the *opy*.

When different groups meet in a village to resolve political issues or hold celebrations, they commonly hold a welcome ritual with music and dancing. These gatherings include conversation, the serving of traditional foods, and collective celebration. In Brazil, groups of young Mbyá singers and dancers have performed at schools and universities. Some groups have recorded songs on CDs, selling them with handicrafts to supplement their income and to spread awareness of the indigenous cause and Mbyá culture.

Knowledge is traditionally transmitted through conversation around the fire, accompanied by drinking maté and smoking a pipe known as a *petyngua*.

## Dance & theatre

The sources describe Mbyá ritual dancing. Shamans lead ritual songs and dances, and welcome rituals involving music and dancing are held when groups meet for political discussions or celebrations.

## Festivals & rituals

One of the Mbyá’s most traditional rituals is the *Ñemongarai*, the child-naming ritual. It takes place during the peak of the maize harvest. A shaman from outside the community names the children of the village. The shaman observes each child’s behavior and attempts to determine which divine being of the Mbyá pantheon sent the child’s spirit. The child is then given a name related to that divine being and its characteristics.

The ritual is understood as the moment when the child’s soul is incorporated into the body and the child becomes Mbyá. The participation of a shaman from outside the community reflects the cultural importance of mobility.

Times of abundance and harvest are generally celebrated with collective rituals when circumstances permit. Meetings between groups may include welcome rituals, music, dancing, traditional food, and conversation. The *opy* is the traditional house of worship in which rituals are performed.

The sources also describe healing and other ritual activities led by *karaí*, *opy'guá*, or “lord of the opy.” These spiritual leaders perform rituals connected with weather, future events, hunting, harvests, songs, dances, and the spiritual names of children.

## Foodways

The Mbyá traditionally hunt, fish, gather food, and plant crops in fields. The principal crops named in the sources are maize, called *avatí*; cassava, called *mandió*; potatoes; peanuts, called *manduí*; beans, called *kumandá*; squash, called *mindain*; and watermelon, called *janjau*. Proto-Guaraní groups relied on planting grains, vegetables, and tubers for nutrition and opened forest clearings with controlled burning.

Mbyá villages are ideally situated near forests, fields, and a good water source, allowing people to obtain resources from the surrounding environment. The sources state that earlier Guaraní groups collected medicinal plants, constructed traps for hunting, and obtained everything they needed from their environment. Contemporary communities increasingly lack sufficient access to these resources and therefore consume industrial products.

Food is also part of collective and ritual life. Knowledge is transmitted through conversation around the fire while drinking maté and smoking a *petyngua*. Meetings and welcome rituals are marked by the serving of traditional foods.

## Oral tradition & literature

The spoken word is central to Mbyá culture. Traditionally, the Mbyá had no writing system, so speech was the means by which customs and knowledge were transmitted. Knowledge was conveyed through conversation around the fire and through rituals in the *opy*. Speech is considered a divine attribute resulting from cosmic inspiration.

In Mbyá tradition, the creator figure is described as a spirit, *nhe’e*, representing speech and eloquence as derived from the gods. Shamans’ telling of creation myths is considered their most important function, and these myths are believed to possess curative power. Verbal dialogue is also the principal means of communication between the Mbyá and the outside world.

The Mbyá language is a mark of group identity. To be considered Mbyá, a person must speak the language and live among family in the community. In Brazil, the Guaraní Project has documented Guaraní culture through the words and actions of Guaraní people and has taught young people methods for documenting their own culture. The project has included documentation of material and non-material culture, photography, and micro-informatics.

## Language & religion

Mbyá Guaraní is a dialect of the Guarani language and is 75% lexically similar to Paraguayan Guarani. It is closely connected to Ava Guarani, also known as Ñandeva, and Mbyá and Ñandeva speakers commonly intermarry. The Mbyá dialect is divided into the *tambèopé* and *baticola* sub-dialects. Many Mbyá speak Mbyá, Paraguayan Guaraní, and Spanish; those living in Brazil often also speak Portuguese.

The sources describe Mbyá religious life through the *opy*, the traditional house of worship; *karaí*, also known as *opy'guá*; ritual songs and dances; creation myths; divine beings; and the spirit *nhe’e*. The Mbyá tradition has incorporated some European-influenced elements, including aspects of Christian eschatology and objects associated with the Jesuits. The sources describe continuing Mbyá shamanism.
